summary: Captures requirements for improved archiving of IETF email lists and for web-based browsing and searching. Participants wanted better search and the existing archive mechanism could be more efficient. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF does its work by email, so the mailing list archives are where the record of that work lives. This RFC lists what a replacement archive and search system has to do: search across any set of lists at once, give every message and every search a shareable web address, import and export the standard mailbox formats, and keep working while one server is down.

subtitle: What a replacement archive for the IETF's mailing lists has to do, so that searching years of discussion is one query.

tldr.problem: Finding one discussion in the IETF's mailing list archives means coordinating several manual searches across lists, because the current tools need a local copy of the archive and do not cover every list.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states the requirements for searching and browsing the archives, for archiving active lists and importing and exporting messages, for redundancy between servers, for administration and for the transition away from the existing MHonArc links.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document rather than a specification. It exists so that a new archive and search system can be built and judged against stated requirements.

facts.label: Searchable attributes
facts.value: 5: sender, date range, Subject, body, message header

facts.label: Initial deployment model
facts.value: Single active and single standby server

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IETF makes heavy use of email lists to conduct its work. Participants frequently need to search the archives of these lists and have asked for improved search capabilities, particularly when the search needs to cover a large period of time or cross several lists. Document editors, shepherds, working group chairs and area directors may need to review all discussion of a particular draft, and that discussion may be spread across the working group list, one or more directorate lists and the IETF general list. Occasionally, work impacts multiple groups, possibly in different areas, and the search must cover additional working group lists.

The current tools for performing these searches require several manually coordinated steps, which are error prone. Without a local copy of the archive, which may not be complete, searching most working group lists requires brute force effort, aided possibly by web search engines. More advanced search capabilities have been constructed for a limited subset of the available lists and are exposed in the 'Email Archives Quick Search' section of the main IETF website, and while these tools are of great assistance there is still significant need for improvement.

The archive mechanism itself could also be made more efficient. The current practices involve duplicate stores, for the web and ftp interfaces, which impact storage and replication and are subject to inconsistency. This memo captures the requirements for improved email list archiving and searching systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF does its work by email, so the mailing list archives are where the record of that work lives. This RFC lists what a replacement archive and search system has to do: search across any set of lists at once, give every message and every search a shareable web address, import and export the standard mailbox formats, and keep working while one server is down.

sections.title: Search and Browsing
sections.content:
The system must provide a web interface for searching and browsing archived messages. It must allow browsing the entire archive of a given list by thread or by date, and it must allow browsing the results of a search by thread or by date. Both threading based on Message-Id, References and In-Reply-To, and threading based on the same subject line, modulo short prefixes such as 're:' and 'fwd:', should be taken into account.

The system must allow searching across any subset of the archived lists: one list, a selection of lists, or all lists. It must allow searching any combination, using AND, OR and NOT operators, of five attributes: a string occurring in the sender name or email address; a date range; a string occurring in the Subject; a string occurring in the message body; and a string occurring in the message header, in particular an exact match of Message-Id. Richer search capabilities are highly desirable. As an illustration of the last of these, the RFC notes it would be nice to search the entire archive for instances of a message with a given Message-ID using a URL of the form http://datatracker.ietf.org/mlarchive/msg?id=4EA6E023.6010603@example.com.

Individual messages must be representable by a long-term stable URI that can be shared between users, that is, a URI suitable for reference in an email message. It would be preferable for that URI to appear in an Archived-At header field in the message. Searches should also be representable by a URI that can be shared, and such URIs should be long-term stable. The search may be re-executed when the URI is referenced, and it is acceptable for the same URI to produce different results if accessed at different times or by different people, for example by reflecting additional messages that match the search criteria, or changes in access authorization to lists with restricted archives.

Access control is stated next. When the system requires credentials, it must use the datatracker's authentication system. While the vast majority of archived lists have an open access policy, some have restricted archives. The system must not require credentials for browsing or searching lists with open archives, although it is acceptable for a user to browse or search such lists while logged in. It must make it possible to limit access to a restricted archive based on login credentials, and messages from restricted archives must be distinguishable from messages from unrestricted archives in any search results.
sections.plainLanguage: Search has to work across lists, not just one, and it has to combine the usual filters with AND, OR and NOT. Every message and every search gets a web address you can paste into an email, and if a list's archive is restricted, the results from it have to be marked as such.

sections.title: Archiving, Importing and Exporting
sections.content:
The archive system must accept messages handled by various mail list manager packages. Lists hosted on the IETF systems are served by Mailman, while lists hosted at other organizations may use other packages, so the archive system must accept messages through subscribing to such an external list, and may support other mechanisms for accepting messages into the archive.

Lists hosted at other systems are sometimes moved to the IETF servers, and their archive is moved with them, so the archiving system must be able to import these archives. At a minimum it must be able to import mbox formatted archives, and it should be able to import Maildir and Maildir-like archives, the key characteristic being one message per file. It is acceptable to use a separate utility to convert between these formats before import, as long as the conversion is lossless.

The archive system must allow both users and administrators to export messages. It must support exporting messages in the mbox format, it should support exporting messages in the Maildir format, it must support exporting the entire archive of a given list, it must support exporting all messages from a given list within a given date range, and it should allow exporting the results of any supported search query.
sections.plainLanguage: The archive has to take mail from whatever list software a list uses, and it has to be able to move an archive in and out in the standard mailbox formats, so that nothing is lost when a list changes hosts.

sections.title: Redundancy, Administration and Transition
sections.content:
The systems must facilitate providing archive, search and browse functions through geographically distributed servers. They must support a single active and single standby server, which reflects the current operating configuration and is expected to be the initial deployment model. They should support a single active and multiple standby servers, and should support multiple active servers for the search and browse functions; support for multiple active archive servers is not a requirement. The amount of traffic generated to ensure data replication between servers should be on the order of the size of any new or changed messages in the archives. It is acceptable for replication to be part of the archival system itself, such as using the replication mechanisms of an underlying database. It is also acceptable to rely on replication of the underlying filesystem objects, using rsync of one or more directory trees for example, but only if the objects in the underlying filesystem are formatted such that the size of the replication data is on the order of the size of any new or changed messages in the archives.

The archive system must support adding and removing lists to be archived. The system must allow the administrator to add messages to and delete messages from an archived list, and should log such actions.

The transition has one requirement. There are many existing archived messages containing embedded links into the existing MHonArc mail archive. These links must continue to work, but they should reach the message as archived in the new system.
sections.plainLanguage: The archive runs on more than one server so it stays up, but only one takes writes at a time, and copying data between servers should cost about as much as the new mail itself. Administrators need to add and remove lists, and old links into the previous archive must keep working.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Creating a new tool for searching and archiving IETF email lists does not affect the security of the Internet in any significant fashion.

Searching can be input and output intensive and CPU intensive. Implementors should consider the potential for maliciously crafted searches attempting to consume all available resources. They should also consider the potential for denial-of-service attacks through making many connections to the browsing system, or rapid navigation within it.

Preserving the integrity of the archives is important. Implementors should ensure that administrative access is appropriately authenticated, and that message paths into the archive are appropriately configured to avoid unauthorized message insertion.
sections.plainLanguage: A search tool that can be asked to do a very expensive query can be turned into a denial-of-service attack, and anyone who can write into the archive can change the record, so the administrative paths need to be authenticated.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ATTRIBUTES A SEARCH MUST COMBINE

items.title: Sender
items.text: A string occurring in the sender name or email address.

items.title: Date range
items.text: A range of dates to search within.

items.title: Subject
items.text: A string occurring in the Subject header.

items.title: Message body
items.text: A string occurring in the body of the message.

items.title: Message header
items.text: A string occurring in the header, in particular an exact match of Message-Id.

viz.caption: THE SERVER MODELS THE ARCHIVE MUST SUPPORT

items.title: Single active, single standby
items.text: Must be supported. This reflects the current operating configuration and is the expected initial deployment model.

items.title: Multiple active for search and browse
items.text: Should be supported. Multiple active archive servers are not a requirement.
